assessment.nobel_worthiness: Systematic formal and empirical analysis of how constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy shape economic outcomes. It created a field, political economics, with wide influence on economics and neighbouring social sciences. It combines rigorous theory with credible empirical tests, and speaks to a central question about why policy and institutions differ across countries.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core pair through their joint theory and the synthesis in the 2000 book, and Besley is a close third through work on state capacity and political selection. Other contributors to the literature (e.g., Acemoglu, already recognised in 2024) are outside this credited set. A three-person grouping is coherent but excludes some adjacent figures.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core work dates from the 1990s and 2000s, and it has been confirmed through decades of citation, replication and extension. There is no timing concern.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions may make the Committee wary of near-term repetition, although this work is distinct in focus on policy-making and electoral rules.
Some of the empirical findings on electoral rules rest on cross-country identification that is less clean than the theory.
Whether Besley or another contributor is the third laureate is a judgment call.
My own field is close to this topic. I have not adjudicated that closeness and mention it only so it can be weighed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data transformed the measurement of intergenerational mobility. It documented large geographic variation and identified causal neighbourhood effects. The work has changed both the research agenda and the policy debate, and it combines novel measurement with credible quasi-experimental design.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure. Hendren (neighbourhood effects and mobility estimates) and Friedman (Opportunity Insights data and tax-record work) are the most plausible co-recipients. Katz's earlier Moving to Opportunity work is also credited in the candidate, so the three-name limit forces a hard choice.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature, but much of the core work is from the 2010s. Replication and long-run follow-up are still accumulating, and some findings are being re-examined.
uncertainties: The younger contributors may be seen as premature by some members.
Methodological debates over the causal interpretation of place effects and over statistical noise in small-area estimates.
Whether a Chetty-centred prize should be split across mobility and tax or public-economics work (see B037).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin modern monetary policy analysis and practice at central banks. Calvo's pricing model, Taylor's rule and staggered-contract work, and Woodford's integrated framework are each widely used and foundational.
assessment.attribution: The credited set is large and the field was built cumulatively. Calvo (price-setting), Taylor (rules and contracts) and Woodford (synthesis and normative analysis) are the clearest foundational trio. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are important for estimation and extension but are more incremental. Any choice leaves out significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. The ideas have been tested through crises and used in policy for decades, and Nobel recognition of core macro-monetary themes is plausible at any time.
uncertainties: Strong disagreement over who deserves priority among the many contributors.
Post-2008 and post-2021 inflation episodes have raised questions about the empirical performance of some of the framework.
Earlier prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Phelps, Sargent-Sims) overlap partly with the territory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference and heterogeneous treatment effects, including double/debiased ML, causal forests and policy learning. They are rapidly becoming standard tools across empirical economics and applied statistics, extending the causal-inference revolution recognised in 2021.
assessment.attribution: Athey and Chernozhukov are the leading economists in the area. Wager has been central to the causal-forest theory, but the proposal stays within two names to keep credit concentrated. Imbens, already recognised, and non-economist statisticians (e.g., Robins, van der Laan) also contributed, so attribution is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The core papers are from roughly 2016 to 2019 and adoption is broad, but the long-run influence on applied results is still being established.
uncertainties: Possibly premature against the track record of earlier methodological prizes.
Credit overlap with statistics and computer science, outside the economics remit.
Athey also appears in the digital-markets candidate (B032), which may divide support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design provide a general framework for optimal information disclosure, linking to mechanism design and communication. They have opened a productive theoretical literature with applications to regulation, platforms and markets.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow originated the persuasion model. Bergemann and Morris generalised it into information design and related it to Bayes correlated equilibrium. Choosing three leaves out one of the four credited names, and the line between originators and generalisers is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Intermediate. The seminal paper is from 2011, the theory is influential, but empirical validation and large-scale applications are still limited.
uncertainties: Limited empirical impact compared with other candidates.
Gentzkow's other work (media economics, text as data) may blur how his credit is framed.
Possible preference for waiting given the recent mechanism-design and auction prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes and wealth have reshaped research and public debate on inequality, and created a major data infrastructure (World Inequality Database). The measurement contribution is substantial, though the work is more descriptive than identified-causal.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the key originators of the top-income series. Zucman extended it to wealth and offshore holdings, but is more junior. Saez also appears in B037 on taxation.
assessment.maturity: Mature for the early top-income series. The wealth-distribution and offshore-wealth parts are newer and still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the measurement of wealth concentration and the treatment of capital income.
Some members may question the theoretical depth of Capital in the Twenty-First Century.
Political salience could be weighed against a record of scientific criteria.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based analysis of technology and the 'China shock' trade-exposure studies changed understanding of labour-market adjustment, wage polarisation and the distributional costs of trade. The findings have been very influential in both research and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure on tasks and polarisation. The trade-shock work was done jointly with Dorn and Hanson. Katz's earlier contributions on skill-biased technology are credited in the candidate but omitted here. Acemoglu's task framework, already recognised in 2024, sits partly outside the credited set.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature, with substantial replication and extension. The 2013 trade-shock paper is still debated.
uncertainties: Debate over the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects and of the identification strategy.
Partial overlap with the 2024 prize and the earlier Card recognition on labour markets.
Whether tasks and trade shocks form one coherent discovery or two.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models revised the transmission mechanisms of monetary and fiscal policy by showing how household heterogeneity and marginal propensities to consume matter for aggregates. They are increasingly used in central banks and academia.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante are jointly credited for the HANK synthesis and the methods. Earlier building blocks, such as Aiyagari and Huggett (incomplete markets) and Krusell-Smith, are outside the credited names and carry priority questions.
assessment.maturity: Relatively early. The central papers date from 2018 and later, and long-run policy validation is limited.
uncertainties: Risk of recognising the synthesis before empirical performance is established.
Priority questions toward the incomplete-markets pioneers.
Possible conflict or familiarity effects with members from macroeconomics.
